results.title: Handling Parallel Trends Violations with `HonestDiD` in R - Tilburg Science Hub
results.content: A common approach to test whether this assumption holds is testing the difference in pre-treatment trends. Here, we cover an alternative approach of Rambachan & Roth (2019), which handles violations of the parallel trends assumption, introducing the `HonestDiD` package in R. This approach identifies the causal effect by assuming the post-treatment difference in trends is precisely similar to the pre-treatment difference. They recognize that while the post-treatment difference in trends between the treated and control groups often may not be exactly the same as the pre-treatment difference, it is similar *to some degree*. The key idea is to restrict the possible values of the post-treatment difference to a certain interval based on the known pre-trend difference. Selecting the right restrictions on how much the pre and post-treatment trends can differ depends on your study's specifics, including the economic context and potential confounding factors. This method uses the pre-treatment to set limits on the post-treatment trend differences, helping us account for any violations. They were concerned about unobserved macroeconomic shocks affecting restaurants (treatment group) differently than other service sectors (control group), leading to a violation of the parallel trends assumption. When you expect the differences in trends between the treatment and control group to evolve smoothly over time without sharp changes, the *Smoothness restriction approach* is appropriate. Title: A selection correction method for heterogeneous treatment effects in staggered adoption settings - ScienceDirect
# A selection correction method for heterogeneous treatment effects in staggered adoption settings. With a selection model, heterogeneous treatment effects are identified. This paper proposes an application of Heckman’s (1979) selection correction approach to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects in staggered adoption settings. With a selection model for treatment timing, selection correction terms in counterfactual trends are derived, and the identified counterfactual trends are plugged into the difference-in-differences parameters. Unlike most methods based on interactive fixed effects models, the proposed method does not require a large number of pre-treatment periods. The empirical relevance of the proposed method is illustrated by estimating the short-term effects of first childbirth timing on women’s labor market outcomes. Recently, the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects has been actively studied in staggered adoption settings. This paper proposes a new application of Heckman’s (1979) selection correction approach to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects. Unlike most methods using interactive fixed effects models, the selection correction method can be applied to setups with a limited number of pre-treatment periods. Recent studies have shown that, in the presence of variation in treatment timing and heterogeneity of treatment effects, the estimation results from two-way fixed effects regressions can provide invalid combinations of average treatment effects (Borusyak et al., 2024, De Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille, 2020, Goodman-Bacon, 2021, Sun and Abraham, 2021). Although the interactive fixed effects models allow non-parallel trends in the counterfactual outcomes, methods based on the interactive fixed effects models generally require a sufficient number of pre-treatment periods. With the parametric models, the treatment effects are identified when parallel trends assumptions are violated due to unobserved confounders and only a limited number of pre-treatment periods is available. This section proposes a selection correction estimator for the heterogeneous treatment effects. This study proposes a new application of Heckman’s (1979) selection correction approach to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects in staggered adoption settings. At the cost of imposing parametric models, the proposed method identifies the treatment effects when non-parallel counterfactual trends include unobserved confounders and a large number of pre-treatment periods is not available. ### Treatment effects in interactive fixed effects models with a small number of time periods.

results.title: Staggered Adoption DiD Designs with Misclassification and Anticipation - ADS
results.content: ## ADS. ## Staggered Adoption DiD Designs with Misclassification and Anticipation. #### Abstract. This paper examines the identification and estimation of treatment effects in staggered adoption designs -- a common extension of the canonical Difference-in-Differences (DiD) model to multiple groups and time-periods -- in the presence of (time varying) misclassification of the treatment status as well as of anticipation. We demonstrate that standard estimators are biased with respect to commonly used causal parameters of interest under such forms of misspecification. To address this issue, we provide modified estimators that recover the Average Treatment Effect of observed and true switching units, respectively. Additionally, we suggest two moment based specification tests aimed at detecting Parallel Trends violations in pre-treatment periods as well as the timing and extent of misclassification and anticipation effects. We illustrate the proposed methods with an application to the effects of an anti-cheating policy on school mean test scores in high stakes national exams in Indonesia. :   10.48550/arXiv.2507.20415.
